rationale: Both prefer a modest meal with peace or friendship to abundant food accompanied by hostility; 17:1 contrasts its pleasant morsel with a house of unjust sacrifices and battle.
source_text: Better a morsel with pleasure in peace than a house full of many good things and unjust sacrifices with battle.

target_units.text: Better hospitality of vegetables with friendship and favor than a serving of calves with enmity.

rationale: The intelligent servant's rule over foolish masters in 17:2 corresponds to the fool serving the intelligent person in 11:29; the former also describes his division of the brothers' portions.
source_text: An intelligent household servant will rule foolish masters, and divide portions among brothers.

target_units.text: One who does not deal well with his own household will inherit wind, and a fool will serve an intelligent person.

rationale: Proverbs places the testing of silver and gold beside hearts chosen before the Lord; Wisdom describes God testing and accepting the righteous like gold in a crucible.
source_text: As silver and gold are tested in a furnace, so hearts are chosen before the Lord.

target_units.text: and after being disciplined a little, they will receive great benefits, because God tested them and found them worthy of Himself.
Like gold in a crucible He tested them, and like a sacrificial whole burnt offering He accepted them.

rationale: The righteous person who ignores lying lips in 17:4 corresponds to the righteous person's hatred of an unjust word in 13:5, contrasting with evil attention to lawless speech.
source_text: An evil person heeds the tongue of lawless people, but a righteous person pays no attention to lying lips.

target_units.text: The righteous hates an unjust word, but the impious is ashamed and will have no frankness.

rationale: Mocking the poor in 17:5 and extorting the needy in 14:31 both provoke their Maker; each saying connects reverence for God with treatment of the poor.
source_text: One who laughs at the poor provokes the One who made him, and one who rejoices over someone perishing will not be acquitted; but one who has compassion will receive mercy.

target_units.text: One who extorts from the needy provokes the One who made him, but one who honors Him has mercy on the poor.

rationale: The final promise that the compassionate will receive mercy corresponds to Jesus' blessing of the merciful because they will receive mercy.
source_text: One who laughs at the poor provokes the One who made him, and one who rejoices over someone perishing will not be acquitted; but one who has compassion will receive mercy.

target_units.text: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.

rationale: Both present grandchildren as a benefit to the older man: a crown in 17:6 and an inheritance in 13:22.
source_text: The crown of elders is children’s children, and the boast of children is their fathers.

target_units.text: A good man will inherit children’s children, but the wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous.

rationale: The proverb assigns the whole world's possessions to the faithful; Paul tells those belonging to Christ that the world and all things are theirs. These are related claims of belonging, without an explicit quotation claim.
source_text: The whole world of possessions belongs to the faithful person, but not even an obol belongs to the unfaithful.

target_units.text: So let no one boast in human beings, for all things are yours,
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, or the world or life or death, or present things or things to come—all are yours,
and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

rationale: The claim that lying lips do not suit the righteous corresponds to 12:22's rejection of lying lips before the Lord and approval of faithful deeds.
source_text: Faithful lips will not suit a fool, nor lying lips a righteous person.

target_units.text: Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but one who performs faithful deeds is acceptable to Him.

rationale: Discipline brings a reward of favors and prosperity to its users in 17:8; 13:18 likewise connects discipline and acceptance of rebukes with escape from dishonor and receipt of glory.
source_text: Discipline is a reward of favors to those who use it, and wherever it turns, it will prosper.

target_units.text: Discipline takes away poverty and dishonor, and one who keeps rebukes will be glorified.

rationale: Proverbs 17:9 connects handling an injustice with preserving or separating friends; 16:28 explicitly attributes the separation of friends to the crooked man's deceitful activity.
source_text: One who hides wrongdoings seeks friendship, but one who hates hiding them separates friends and household members.

target_units.text: A crooked man sends out evils, lights a torch of deceit for evil people, and separates friends.

rationale: The fool who fails to perceive even when whipped in 17:10 corresponds to the fool whose foolishness remains despite public whipping in 27:22.
source_text: A threat crushes an intelligent person’s heart, but a fool, though whipped, does not perceive.

target_units.text: If you whip a fool in the midst of a council, dishonoring him, you will certainly not strip away his foolishness.

rationale: Proverbs 17:11 threatens a dispute-maker with the Lord's merciless messenger; 16:14 pictures a king's wrath as a messenger of death. Both use a punitive messenger image, with different senders.
source_text: Every evil person raises disputes, but the Lord will send a merciless messenger to him.

target_units.text: A king’s wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will appease him.

rationale: The proverb condemns repaying good with evil; the psalmist complains that his opponents exchanged his good deeds for evils and his love for hatred.
source_text: One who repays evil things instead of good things—evils will not move from his house.

target_units.text: They set evils against me in exchange for good things and hatred in exchange for my love.

rationale: The proverb rejects both acquitting the unjust and condemning the righteous; Exodus forbids unrighteous charges, killing the innocent or righteous, and justifying the ungodly for gifts.
source_text: One who judges the unjust righteous and the righteous unjust is unclean and detestable before God.

target_units.text: You shall keep far away from every unrighteous charge; the innocent and the righteous you shall not kill, neither shall you justify the ungodly for gifts.

rationale: Proverbs 17:16 denies that a fool's wealth enables him to acquire wisdom; 14:6 likewise says wisdom will not be found among evil people, contrasting the discernment available among the intelligent.
source_text: Why did possessions come to a fool? For one lacking heart will not be able to acquire wisdom.

target_units.text: You will seek wisdom among evil people and not find it, but discernment is readily found among intelligent people.

rationale: The warning that turning crookedly away from learning brings evils corresponds to 15:10's warning that those who hate rebukes die shamefully.
source_text: One who makes his own house high seeks ruin, and one who turns crookedly away from learning will fall into evils.

target_units.text: The discipline of an innocent person is recognized by passersby, but those who hate rebukes die shamefully.

rationale: The enduring friend and the brother useful in need in 17:17 can be read with 27:10's counsel to keep one's friend and its preference for a nearby friend over a distant brother in misfortune.
source_text: Let a friend be yours at all times, and let brothers be useful in times of need; for this is why they are born.

target_units.text: Do not abandon your friend or an ancestral friend, and do not enter your brother’s house when misfortune strikes you; a nearby friend is better than a brother dwelling far away.

rationale: The guarantor's pledge for a friend in 17:18 corresponds to the guarantee in 6:1-3, which describes giving one's hand over to an enemy, entrapment by one's own lips and the need to seek release.
source_text: A foolish man claps and rejoices over himself, as does one who acts as guarantor for his own friend with a pledge.

target_units.text: Son, if you act as guarantor for your friend, you will give your hand over to an enemy.
For a man’s own lips are a strong trap, and he is caught by the lips of his own mouth.
Son, do what I command you and save yourself—for through your friend you have come into evil men’s hands. Go without growing slack, and press the friend for whom you acted as guarantor.

rationale: Proverbs 17:19 joins love of sin to delight in battles; 29:22 likewise connects wrath with digging up strife and anger with digging out sins.
source_text: One who loves sin rejoices in battles,

target_units.text: A wrathful man digs up strife, and an angry man dug out sins.

rationale: The hard-hearted person who fails to meet good in 17:20 corresponds to the hard-hearted person who falls into evils in 28:14.
source_text: but one hard of heart does not meet good things. A man changeable in tongue will fall into evils,

target_units.text: Happy is a man who shrinks from everything out of reverence, but one hard of heart will fall into evils.

rationale: The foolish son brings his father no joy in 17:21, while an intelligent son gladdens his mother; 10:1 also contrasts the wise son's parental joy with the foolish son's parental grief.
source_text: and a fool’s heart is pain to the one who possesses it. A father does not rejoice over an uneducated son, but an intelligent son gladdens his mother.

target_units.text: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is grief to his mother.

rationale: Both describe the heart's emotional condition through bodily effects: joy produces flourishing, while sorrow produces gloom in 15:13 and dried bones in 17:22.
source_text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

target_units.text: When the heart rejoices, the face flourishes, but when it is in sorrows, the face grows gloomy.

rationale: The drying of a sorrowful man's bones contrasts with the good report that makes bones full; both sayings also connect good experiences with a glad or flourishing heart.
source_text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

target_units.text: An eye looking at good things gladdens the heart, and a good report makes bones full.

rationale: Gifts taken unjustly in a person's lap and the bending of righteous ways correspond to Exodus's warning that received gifts blind the seeing and corrupt righteous words.
source_text: The ways of one taking gifts unjustly in his lap do not prosper, and an impious person bends the ways of righteousness.

target_units.text: And you shall receive no gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of those who see, and corrupt righteous words.

rationale: The ways of someone taking gifts unjustly do not prosper in 17:23; 15:27 likewise warns that taking bribes destroys their recipient.
source_text: The ways of one taking gifts unjustly in his lap do not prosper, and an impious person bends the ways of righteousness.

target_units.text: One who takes bribes destroys himself, but one who hates taking gifts is saved.

rationale: The foolish son's anger for his father and pain for his mother develop the family grief attributed to a foolish son in 10:1.
source_text: A foolish son is anger to a father, and pain to the one who bore him.

target_units.text: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is grief to his mother.

rationale: The prohibition on penalizing the righteous and plotting against righteous rulers shares Exodus's protection of the innocent and righteous from an unjust charge and killing.
source_text: To penalize a righteous man is not good, nor is it holy to plot against righteous rulers.

target_units.text: You shall keep far away from every unrighteous charge; the innocent and the righteous you shall not kill, neither shall you justify the ungodly for gifts.

rationale: Both explicitly connect patience with understanding: 17:27 associates restraint from harsh words with discernment, while 14:29 calls the patient man great in understanding.
source_text: One who refrains from sending forth a harsh word is discerning, and a patient man is intelligent.

target_units.text: A patient man is great in understanding, but one faint of spirit is exceedingly foolish.

rationale: Avoiding a harsh word in 17:27 accords with 15:1's contrast between the yielding answer that turns wrath away and the painful word that stirs anger.
source_text: One who refrains from sending forth a harsh word is discerning, and a patient man is intelligent.

target_units.text: Anger destroys even intelligent people; but a yielding answer turns away wrath, and a painful word stirs up anger.

rationale: Proverbs 11:12 associates intelligence with keeping quiet; 17:28 says that making oneself mute makes one appear intelligent.
source_text: Wisdom will be reckoned to a senseless person who asks for wisdom, and someone who makes himself mute will seem intelligent.

target_units.text: One lacking understanding sneers at citizens, but an intelligent man keeps quiet.

rationale: The person who separates from friends seeks pretexts and invites reproach in 18:1; 27:10 gives the opposing instruction not to abandon one's friend or ancestral friend.
source_text: A man who wishes to separate from friends seeks pretexts, and at every time he will be subject to reproach.

target_units.text: Do not abandon your friend or an ancestral friend, and do not enter your brother’s house when misfortune strikes you; a nearby friend is better than a brother dwelling far away.

rationale: The fool who has no use for wisdom in 18:2 corresponds to the person called foolish for hating rebukes in 12:1, in contrast to love for discipline and discernment.
source_text: One lacking understanding has no use for wisdom, for he is led rather by foolishness.

target_units.text: One who loves discipline loves discernment, but one who hates rebukes is foolish.

rationale: Both compare content of a man's heart to deep water; 18:4 describes a word and the springing of a river and fountain, while 20:5 describes counsel drawn out by an intelligent man.
source_text: A word in a man’s heart is deep water, and a river springs up, a fountain of life.

target_units.text: Counsel in a man’s heart is deep water, but an intelligent man will draw it out.

rationale: Admiring the impious person's face and perverting judgment in 18:5 corresponds to the declaration in 24:23 that deference to a face in judgment is not good.
source_text: To admire the face of the impious is not good, nor is it holy to turn aside what is just in judgment.

target_units.text: These things I say to you, the wise, to recognize: to show deference to a face in judgment is not good;

rationale: The rash mouth that calls for death in 18:6 corresponds to the rash person's mouth drawing near to ruin in 10:14.
source_text: A fool’s lips lead him into evils, and his rash mouth calls upon death.

target_units.text: Wise people will hide discernment, but the mouth of a rash person draws near to ruin.

rationale: The fool's lips trap his life in 18:7; in 12:13 the sinner falls into traps through the sin of his lips. Both connect harmful speech with danger to its speaker.
source_text: A fool’s mouth is ruin for him, and his lips are a trap for his life.

target_units.text: Through the sin of lips a sinner falls into traps, but the righteous escapes from them.

rationale: Both sayings associate disabling fear or cowardice with idleness and hunger; 18:8's hunger statement corresponds to 19:15's explicit warning that the idle person's life will hunger.
source_text: Fear casts down the lazy, and the lives of womanish men will hunger.

target_units.text: Cowardice holds a womanish man, and the life of an idle person will hunger.

rationale: Running to the strength of the Lord's name and being raised high corresponds to the psalmist being raised upon a rock and calling God a tower of strength before the enemy.
source_text: From greatness of strength comes the name of the Lord, and righteous people who run to it are raised high.

target_units.text: From the ends of the earth I cried unto Thee when my heart grew weary; Thou didst raise me upon a rock,
Thou didst guide me, for Thou becamest my hope, a tower of strength before the enemy.

rationale: Both expressly picture the rich person's possessions as a fortified city; 18:11 adds the image of a great shadow to this portrayal of wealth as security.
source_text: A rich man’s property is a fortified city, and its glory casts a great shadow.

target_units.text: The possession of the rich is a fortified city, but the ruin of the impious is poverty.

rationale: The heart's pride before ruin in 18:12 corresponds to insolence before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall in 16:18.
source_text: Before ruin a man’s heart is raised high, and before glory it is humbled.

target_units.text: Insolence leads before ruin, and evil-mindedness before a fall.

rationale: Both pair pride or insolence bringing a person low with humility leading to glory; 29:23 expressly identifies the Lord as supporting the humble-minded.
source_text: Before ruin a man’s heart is raised high, and before glory it is humbled.

target_units.text: Insolence brings a man low, but the Lord supports the humble-minded with glory.

rationale: Answering before hearing is called folly in Proverbs; James gives the corresponding positive counsel to be quick to hear and slow to speak.
source_text: One who answers a word before hearing it—it is foolishness and reproach for him.

target_units.text: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,

rationale: The intelligent attendant who calms anger in 18:14 corresponds to the gentle-tempered man called a physician of the heart in 14:30. Both describe another person's temperate care as relieving distress.
source_text: An intelligent attendant calms a man’s anger, but who will bear a fainthearted man?

target_units.text: A gentle-tempered man is a physician of the heart, but a perceptive heart is a moth to the bones.

rationale: The intelligent heart acquiring discernment in 18:15 repeats the association between an upright heart and seeking discernment in 15:14.
source_text: An intelligent heart acquires discernment, and the ears of the wise seek reflection.

target_units.text: An upright heart seeks discernment, but the mouth of the uneducated will know evil things.

rationale: A gift makes room for its giver and seats him with rulers in 18:16; 25:6-7 distinguishes being invited upward from presumptuously taking a ruler's place. Both concern access and seating before rulers.
source_text: A person’s gift makes space for him, and seats him beside rulers.

target_units.text: Do not boast before a king, and do not station yourself in the places of rulers;
for it is better for you to be told, “Come up to me,” than for him to humble you before a ruler. Say what your eyes have seen.

rationale: Proverbs describes a lot making a determination among rulers; Acts records a lot determining which proposed man would take the vacant place among the apostles after prayer.
source_text: A lot stops disputes, and makes a determination among rulers.

target_units.text: They put forward two: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also named Justus, and Matthias.
They prayed and said, “Thou, Lord, who knowest everyone’s heart, show which one of these two Thou hast chosen
to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.”
They cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles.

rationale: The brother helped by a brother is compared to a fortified city in 18:19; 17:17 identifies brothers as useful in need. Each describes the practical security of mutual kinship aid.
source_text: A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified and high city, and is strong like a founded palace.

target_units.text: Let a friend be yours at all times, and let brothers be useful in times of need; for this is why they are born.

rationale: Both describe filling from the fruit of mouth or lips; 18:20 names a filled belly, while 12:14 speaks of good things filling the life and of recompense from the lips.
source_text: From fruits of a mouth a man fills his belly, and from fruits of his lips he will be filled.

target_units.text: From fruits of a mouth a man’s life will be filled with good things, and the recompense of his lips will be given to him.

rationale: The tongue's power over death and life in 18:21 corresponds to 12:18's contrast between speech that wounds like a sword and the wise tongue that heals.
source_text: Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who control it will eat its fruits.

target_units.text: There are those who wound with a sword as they speak, but the tongues of the wise heal.

rationale: Finding a good wife brings favor and gladness from God in 18:22; 19:14 attributes the joining of wife and husband to God, distinguishing it from inherited possessions.
source_text: One who found a good wife found favors, and received gladness from God.

target_units.text: Fathers apportion house and property to children, but a wife is joined to a husband by God.

rationale: Casting out a good wife and retaining an adulteress is condemned in 18:22a; 5:18-20 instead urges delight in the wife of one's youth and rejects embracing another woman.
source_text: One who casts out a good wife casts out good things, but one who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious.

target_units.text: Let your fountain of water be your own, and share joy with the wife of your youth.

Let a deer of affection and a colt of your graces keep company with you. Let your own woman lead you and be with you at every time, for as you move in the company of her affection, you will be one among many.
Do not be much involved with another woman, nor be held in the arms of one who is not your own.

rationale: The person whose own folly ruins his ways nevertheless blames God in Proverbs; James rejects blaming God for temptation and traces temptation and sin to one's own desire.
source_text: A man’s foolishness ruins his ways, but in his heart he blames God.

target_units.text: Let no one who is tempted say, “I am being tempted by God.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself tempts no one.
But each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire.
Then desire, after conceiving, gives birth to sin; and sin, when fully grown, gives birth to death.

rationale: Both contrast the many friends associated with wealth against the abandonment or hatred experienced by a poor friend.
source_text: Wealth adds many friends, but the poor person is abandoned even by the friend he has.

target_units.text: Friends will hate poor friends, but the friends of the rich are many.

rationale: Proverbs warns that a false witness and unjust accuser will not escape; Exodus forbids receiving an empty report or agreeing with the unrighteous to become an unrighteous witness.
source_text: A false witness will not be unpunished, and one who accuses unjustly will not escape.

target_units.text: “You shall not receive an empty report. You shall not agree with the unrighteous to become an unrighteous witness.

rationale: The many who attend kings' faces in 19:6 correspond to the many who court leaders' faces in 29:26; the latter adds that a person's justice comes from the Lord.
source_text: Many attend the faces of kings, but every evil person becomes a reproach to a man.

target_units.text: Many court the faces of leaders, but what is just for a man comes from the Lord.

rationale: The opening description of hatred toward a poor brother and estrangement from friendship corresponds to the hatred experienced by poor friends in 14:20.
source_text: Everyone who hates a poor brother will also be far from friendship. A good thought will draw near to those who know it, and an intelligent man will find it. One who does many evils brings wickedness to completion, and one who provokes words will not be saved.

target_units.text: Friends will hate poor friends, but the friends of the rich are many.

rationale: Acquiring and preserving understanding is described as loving oneself in 19:8; 15:32 likewise describes keeping rebukes as loving one's own life, against rejecting discipline.
source_text: One who acquires understanding loves himself, and one who keeps understanding will find good things.

target_units.text: One who thrusts discipline away hates himself, but one who keeps rebukes loves his own life.

rationale: The keeper of understanding who finds good things in 19:8 corresponds to the understanding person explicitly called a finder of good things in 16:20.
source_text: One who acquires understanding loves himself, and one who keeps understanding will find good things.

target_units.text: One understanding in matters is a finder of good things, and one trusting in God is blessed.

rationale: Both sayings begin with the warning that a false witness will not go unpunished; their second clauses develop the destructive outcome of wrongful accusation or kindled wickedness.
source_text: A false witness will not be unpunished, and whoever kindles wickedness will perish by it.

target_units.text: A false witness will not be unpunished, and one who accuses unjustly will not escape.

rationale: The fool's inappropriate luxury and the servant's insolent rule in 19:10 correspond to the unsettling examples of a fool filled with food and a household servant becoming king in 30:21-23.
source_text: Luxury does not benefit a fool, nor does it benefit a household servant if he begins to rule with insolence.

target_units.text: Through three things the earth is shaken, and it cannot bear the fourth:
if a household servant becomes king, and a fool is filled with food,
and if a maidservant casts out her own mistress, and if a hated woman obtains a good husband.

rationale: The merciful person's patience in 19:11 corresponds to love described together as patient and kind in 1 Corinthians; the link concerns those joined qualities.
source_text: A merciful man is patient, and his boast comes upon lawless people.

target_units.text: Love is patient; love is kind; it does not envy; [love] does not boast, is not puffed up,

rationale: Both compare a king's threatening power to a lion; 19:12 also contrasts that threat with his cheerfulness like dew, while 20:2 stresses the danger of provoking him.
source_text: A king’s threat is like a lion’s growling, but as dew upon grass, so is his cheerfulness.

target_units.text: A king’s threat does not differ at all from a lion’s wrath, and one who provokes him sins against his own life.

rationale: The foolish son who brings shame to his father in 19:13 corresponds to the foolish son's parental grief in 10:1; the connection concerns the first clause of 19:13.
source_text: A foolish son is shame to a father, and prayers from a courtesan’s fee are not pure.

target_units.text: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is grief to his mother.

rationale: Proverbs calls prayers associated with a courtesan's fee impure; Deuteronomy forbids bringing a prostitute's hire into the Lord's house for a vow.
source_text: A foolish son is shame to a father, and prayers from a courtesan’s fee are not pure.

target_units.text: You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute, nor the price of a dog, into the house of the Lord your God for any vow; for both are an abomination unto the Lord your God.

rationale: God's joining of wife and husband in 19:14 corresponds to the favor and gladness from God associated with finding a good wife in 18:22.
source_text: Fathers apportion house and property to children, but a wife is joined to a husband by God.

target_units.text: One who found a good wife found favors, and received gladness from God.

rationale: The connection of cowardice, idleness and hunger in 19:15 corresponds to the disabling fear and hunger associated with the lazy in 18:8.
source_text: Cowardice holds a womanish man, and the life of an idle person will hunger.

target_units.text: Fear casts down the lazy, and the lives of womanish men will hunger.

rationale: Keeping the command guards one's life in 19:16, while despising one's ways brings death; 16:17 similarly joins disciplined, righteous ways and guarding one's ways to preservation of life.
source_text: One who keeps a command guards his own life, but one who despises his own ways will perish.

target_units.text: Paths of life turn aside from evils, and ways of righteousness are length of life. One who receives discipline will be amid good things, and one who keeps rebukes will be made wise. One who guards his own ways keeps his own life, and one who loves his life will spare his mouth.

rationale: Showing mercy to the poor is a loan God will repay in 19:17; 28:27 similarly promises that one who gives to the poor will not be in need.
source_text: One who has mercy on the poor lends to God, and He will repay him according to his gift.

target_units.text: One who gives to the poor will not be in need; but one who turns away his eye will be in great difficulty.

rationale: The instruction to discipline a son so that he will be hopeful corresponds to the careful discipline attributed to a parent's love in 13:24.
source_text: Discipline your son, for in this way he will be hopeful, but do not lift yourself in your soul toward insolence.

target_units.text: One who spares the staff hates his son, but one who loves him disciplines carefully.

rationale: The command to listen to a father's discipline so as to become wise in later days corresponds to 4:1's appeal to children to hear paternal discipline and attend to understanding.
source_text: Listen, son, to your father’s discipline, so that you may become wise in your latter days.

target_units.text: Listen, children, to a father’s discipline; pay attention to gain discernment,

rationale: Human reasonings are many but the Lord's counsel endures in 19:21; 21:1 pictures even a king's heart in God's hand and inclined wherever He wills.
source_text: Many are the reasonings in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains for ever.

target_units.text: As a rush of water, so is a king’s heart in God’s hand; wherever He willingly inclines, there He has bent it.

rationale: The righteous poor person is preferred to a rich liar in 19:22, corresponding to 28:6's preference for a poor person walking in truth over a lying rich person.
source_text: Mercy is a man’s fruit, and better a righteous poor person than a rich liar.

target_units.text: Better a poor person walking in truth than a lying rich person.

relationship: fear of the Lord and life
rationale: The fear of the Lord is directed toward life in 19:23; 10:27 similarly says that it adds days, in contrast to the shortened years of the impious.
source_text: The fear of the Lord is for a man’s life, but the fearless person will lodge in places where knowledge is not attended to.

target_units.text: The fear of the Lord adds days, but the years of the impious will become few.

rationale: Both portray hands hidden in a lap and failure to bring them to the mouth. Proverbs 19:24 calls the hiding unjust, while 26:15 assigns the image to a lazy person.
source_text: One who unjustly hides his hands in his lap will certainly not even bring them to his mouth.

target_units.text: A lazy person, having hidden his hand in his lap, will not be able to bring it to his mouth.

rationale: Both describe an undisciplined or pestilent person's punishment teaching an observer, and then contrast the knowledge received by an intelligent or wise person.
source_text: When a pestilent person is whipped, a fool becomes more resourceful; but if you reprove an intelligent man, he will understand discernment.

target_units.text: When an undisciplined person is penalized, the innocent becomes more resourceful, and a wise person who understands will receive knowledge.

rationale: The child who dishonors his father and thrusts away his mother corresponds to the one who casts away father or mother while denying the sin in 28:24.
source_text: One who dishonors a father and thrusts his mother away will be put to shame and be subject to reproach.

target_units.text: One who casts away a father or mother and thinks he is not sinning is a partner of an impious man.

rationale: Neglecting a father's discipline leads to meditation on evil sayings in 19:27; 15:5 similarly identifies sneering at a father's discipline with foolishness.
source_text: A son who falls short of keeping a father’s discipline will meditate on evil sayings.

target_units.text: A fool sneers at a father’s discipline, but one who keeps commands is more resourceful.

rationale: Both criticize taking on a guarantee: 19:28 calls guaranteeing a foolish child insolence toward just judgment, while 17:18 compares a friend's guarantor with a foolish man's self-rejoicing.
source_text: One who acts as guarantor for a foolish child treats just judgment with insolence, and the mouth of the impious swallows judgments.

target_units.text: A foolish man claps and rejoices over himself, as does one who acts as guarantor for his own friend with a pledge.

rationale: Whips and punishments are assigned to the undisciplined and fools in 19:29; 26:3 compares a rod for a lawless nation to the whip and goad used for animals.
source_text: Whips are prepared for the undisciplined, and punishments for the shoulders of fools.

target_units.text: As a whip for a horse and a goad for a donkey, so a rod for a lawless nation.

rationale: Proverbs opposes drunken insolence to wisdom; Ephesians joins its warning against foolishness to a command against drunkenness with wine and its reckless excess.
source_text: Wine is undisciplined, and drunkenness insolent, and everyone who mingles with it will not be wise.

target_units.text: For this reason do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is reckless excess, but be filled in the Spirit,

rationale: Both depict a king's threat as a lion's wrath or growling; 20:2 explicitly warns that provoking this threat endangers one's life.
source_text: A king’s threat does not differ at all from a lion’s wrath, and one who provokes him sins against his own life.

target_units.text: A king’s threat is like a lion’s growling, but as dew upon grass, so is his cheerfulness.

rationale: Turning away from abuse brings glory in 20:3, while a fool becomes entangled in it; 15:18 similarly contrasts a patient person's calming of battle with a quick-tempered person's creation of it.
source_text: It is glory for a man to turn away from abuse, but every fool entangles himself in such things.

target_units.text: A quick-tempered man prepares battles, but a patient person calms even a battle about to begin.

rationale: Both picture something within a person's heart as deep water: counsel drawn out by an intelligent man in 20:5, and a word that becomes a river and fountain in 18:4.
source_text: Counsel in a man’s heart is deep water, but an intelligent man will draw it out.

target_units.text: A word in a man’s heart is deep water, and a river springs up, a fountain of life.

rationale: The difficulty of finding a faithful man corresponds to the psalm's lament that truths have become few and neighbors speak deceitfully. The proverb's praise of humanity and mercy remains its own setting.
source_text: A human being is a great thing, and a merciful man a precious thing, but finding a faithful man is hard work.

target_units.text: Save me, Lord, for the holy one is gone; for truths have become few among the sons of men.
Each spoke empty things to his neighbor; deceitful lips spoke with a heart and a heart.

rationale: The blameless person's righteousness leaves his children blessed in 20:7; 14:26 similarly connects fear of the Lord with leaving support for one's children.
source_text: One who lives blamelessly in righteousness will leave his children blessed.

target_units.text: In the fear of the Lord is hope of strength, and he leaves a support for his children.

rationale: The righteous king before whom no evil stands in 20:8 corresponds to 25:5's removal of impious people from before a king so that his throne prospers in righteousness.
source_text: When a righteous king sits on a throne, no evil thing sets itself against him before his eyes.

target_units.text: Kill the impious from before a king, and his throne will prosper in righteousness.

rationale: The challenge to boast of a pure heart or freedom from sins corresponds to Solomon's acknowledgement that there is no person who will not sin.
source_text: Who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will speak confidently of being clean from sins?

target_units.text: “When they sin against Thee—for there is no person who will not sin—and Thou bringest trouble upon them and givest them over before enemies, and their captors carry them away to a land far and near,

rationale: Both link dishonoring parents with a judgment pictured through the eyes: darkness in 20:9a, and the mocking eye being pecked out in 30:17.
source_text: The lamp of one who speaks evil of a father or mother will be extinguished, and the pupils of his eyes will see darkness.

target_units.text: An eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age—may ravens from the ravines peck it out, and may young eagles devour it.

rationale: An eagerly pursued portion ends without blessing in 20:9b; 13:11 likewise warns that eagerly pursued property becomes less, specifically describing that pursuit as lawless.
source_text: A portion eagerly pursued at first will not be blessed at the end.

target_units.text: Property pursued eagerly with lawlessness becomes less, but one who gathers for himself with piety will increase; a righteous person has compassion and lends.

rationale: Proverbs forbids saying one will punish the enemy and directs waiting for the Lord's help; Romans similarly forbids self-avenging and reserves repayment to the Lord.
source_text: Do not say, “I will punish the enemy.” But wait for the Lord, so that He may help you.

target_units.text: Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but make room for wrath; for it is written, “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”

rationale: The rejection of unequal weights and double measures before the Lord corresponds to 11:1's rejection of deceitful scales and approval of a just weight.
source_text: A large weight and a small one, and double measures—both are unclean before the Lord.

target_units.text: Deceitful scales are an abomination before the Lord, but a just weight is acceptable to Him.

rationale: In the context of 20:10's false measures, their maker is fettered in his practices; 5:22 similarly pictures a man bound tightly by the cords of his own sins.
source_text: And one who makes them will be fettered in his practices; a young man is with a devout person, and his way is straight.

target_units.text: Lawless acts hunt a man, and each is bound tight by the cords of his own sins.

rationale: The ear and eye are both works of the Lord in Proverbs; the psalm argues from God's planting of the ear and forming of the eye that He hears and perceives.
source_text: An ear hears and an eye sees; both are works of the Lord.

target_units.text: Does the One who planted the ear not hear, or the One who formed the eye not perceive?

rationale: The warning against speaking against others lest one be cut off corresponds to 13:3's connection between guarding one's mouth and preserving one's life.
source_text: Do not love speaking against others, so that you are not cut off; open your eyes and be filled with loaves.

target_units.text: One who guards his own mouth keeps his own life, but one rash with his lips will terrify himself.

rationale: Both condemn deceitful scales before the Lord; 20:23 also explicitly names the double weight as an abomination.
source_text: A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and deceitful scales are not good before Him.

target_units.text: Deceitful scales are an abomination before the Lord, but a just weight is acceptable to Him.

rationale: A person's steps directed by the Lord in 20:24 correspond to the steps set right by God in 15:29b, where the heart is told to consider righteous things.
source_text: A man’s steps are directed by the Lord, but how could a mortal understand his ways?

target_units.text: Let a man’s heart consider righteous things, so that his steps may be set right by God.

rationale: The trap of consecrating something quickly and regretting the vow corresponds to Ecclesiastes' counsel to pay what one vows and its preference for not vowing over vowing without payment.
source_text: It is a trap for a man quickly to consecrate something of his own, for after making the vow comes reconsideration.

target_units.text: Whenever you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for there is no delight in fools. Pay whatever you vow.
Better that you do not vow than that you vow and do not pay.
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before God, “It was ignorance,” lest God become angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands.

rationale: The wise king's winnowing of the impious corresponds to 25:5's removal of the impious from before a king so that his throne prospers in righteousness.
source_text: A wise king is a winnower of the impious, and will bring a wheel upon them.

target_units.text: Kill the impious from before a king, and his throne will prosper in righteousness.

relationship: divine scrutiny of the inward person
rationale: Proverbs describes the Lord searching the belly's inward chambers; Jeremiah similarly has the Lord examine hearts and test kidneys before giving each person according to his ways.
source_text: The breath of human beings is the light of the Lord, who searches the store-chambers of the belly.

target_units.text: I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

rationale: Mercy and truth surround the king's throne in righteousness in 20:28; 29:14 likewise connects the establishment of his throne with judging the poor in truth.
source_text: Mercy and truth are a guard for a king, and they will surround his throne in righteousness.

target_units.text: When a king judges the poor in truth, his throne will be established as a testimony.

rationale: Gray hair as the elders' glory corresponds to old age as a crown of boasting in 16:31; the link concerns the elderly, while 20:29 separately praises young men's wisdom.
source_text: Wisdom is an adornment for young men, and gray hair is the glory of elders.

target_units.text: Old age is a crown of boasting, and it is found in ways of righteousness.

rationale: The bruises, wounds and blows assigned to evil people in 20:30 correspond to the whips and punishments prepared for the undisciplined and fools in 19:29.
source_text: Bruises and crushing wounds meet evil people, and blows reach the store-chambers of the belly.

target_units.text: Whips are prepared for the undisciplined, and punishments for the shoulders of fools.

rationale: The proverb pictures a king's heart inclined by God; Ezra gives a narrative example when the Lord stirs Cyrus's spirit and the king announces the commission to build God's house.
source_text: As a rush of water, so is a king’s heart in God’s hand; wherever He willingly inclines, there He has bent it.

target_units.text: In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, so that the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians. He ordered a proclamation throughout his kingdom, also in writing, saying:
“Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord, God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and He has charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem in Judea.

rationale: A person appearing righteous to himself in 21:2 corresponds to fools' ways appearing upright before them in 12:15, which contrasts that self-assessment with listening to counsel.
source_text: Every man appears righteous to himself, but the Lord sets hearts straight.

target_units.text: The ways of fools are upright before them, but a wise person listens to counsel.

rationale: Proverbs contrasts human self-approval with the Lord setting hearts straight; Jeremiah contrasts the heart's depth beyond human knowledge with the Lord examining it and judging its ways.
source_text: Every man appears righteous to himself, but the Lord sets hearts straight.

target_units.text: The heart is deep beyond all things, and so is a human; and who will know him?
I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

rationale: Both expressly place doing righteous things above offering sacrifices in God's estimation; 21:3 additionally names speaking truth and the blood of sacrifices.
source_text: Doing righteous things and speaking truth are more pleasing before God than the blood of sacrifices.

target_units.text: The beginning of a good way is to do righteous things, and these are more acceptable before God than sacrificing sacrifices.

rationale: The insolent, lofty-minded and rash-hearted person in 21:4 corresponds to the high-hearted person declared unclean before God in 16:5.
source_text: One lofty-minded in insolence is rash-hearted, and the lamp of the impious is sin.

target_units.text: Everyone high of heart is unclean before God, and one who unjustly puts hands into a hand will not be acquitted.

rationale: Accumulating stores through a false tongue leads toward emptiness and death traps in 21:6; 13:11 likewise warns that property eagerly pursued with lawlessness diminishes.
source_text: One who works up stores with a false tongue pursues empty things toward traps of death.

target_units.text: Property pursued eagerly with lawlessness becomes less, but one who gathers for himself with piety will increase; a righteous person has compassion and lends.

rationale: Destruction comes upon those unwilling to do righteous things in 21:7; 11:6 similarly describes lawless people caught in their own destruction, in contrast to the rescue righteousness brings.
source_text: Destruction will lodge with the impious, for they do not wish to do righteous things.

target_units.text: The righteousness of upright men rescues them, but lawless people are caught in their own destruction.

rationale: God sends crooked ways to crooked people while His works remain upright; the psalm similarly describes God's dealings corresponding to the holy, innocent, chosen and twisted person.
source_text: God sends crooked ways to the crooked, for His works are pure and upright.

target_units.text: With a holy one Thou wilt show Thyself holy, and with an innocent man Thou wilt be innocent,
and with a chosen one Thou wilt be chosen, and with a twisted one Thou wilt twist.

rationale: Both prefer an exposed corner to a shared house: 21:9 contrasts its corner with injustice in plastered rooms, while 25:24 contrasts a roof corner with an abusive wife.
source_text: Better to dwell on a corner in the open air than in plastered rooms with injustice and in a shared house.

target_units.text: Better to dwell on a corner of a roof than with an abusive wife in a shared house.

rationale: Both describe another person's punishment instructing an observer, then contrast this with the knowledge an intelligent or wise person receives through understanding or reproof.
source_text: When an undisciplined person is penalized, the innocent becomes more resourceful, and a wise person who understands will receive knowledge.

target_units.text: When a pestilent person is whipped, a fool becomes more resourceful; but if you reprove an intelligent man, he will understand discernment.

rationale: Closing one's ears to the weak results in an unanswered call in 21:13; turning one's eye away from the poor results in great difficulty in 28:27.
source_text: One who blocks his ears from hearing the weak will himself also call, and there will be no one listening.

target_units.text: One who gives to the poor will not be in need; but one who turns away his eye will be in great difficulty.

rationale: The gift that overturns anger in Proverbs corresponds to Jacob's stated hope that gifts sent before him will appease Esau and lead Esau to accept him.
source_text: A secret gift overturns anger, but one who is sparing with gifts raises fierce wrath.

target_units.text: “And you shall say, ‘Behold, your servant Jacob comes behind us.’” For he said, “I will appease him with the gifts going before him, and afterward I shall see his face; for perhaps he will accept me.”

rationale: The devout person regarded as unclean by evildoers in 21:15 corresponds to the straightening way regarded as an abomination by the lawless in 29:27.
source_text: Doing judgment is the joy of the righteous, but a devout person is unclean in the eyes of evildoers.

target_units.text: An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but a straightening way is an abomination to a lawless person.

rationale: Leaving righteousness leads to rest among the giants in 21:16; 2:18 places the house of personified evil counsel, identified in 2:17, beside death and its courses beside Hades with the earthborn.
source_text: A man who wanders from the way of righteousness will rest in the assembly of giants.

target_units.text: For she has set her house beside death and her courses beside Hades with the earthborn.

rationale: The lawless person as a cleansing-offering for the righteous in 21:18 corresponds to the impious person handed over in the righteous person's place after the righteous escapes in 11:8.
source_text: but a lawless person is a cleansing-offering for the righteous.

target_units.text: The righteous escapes from the hunt, but the impious is handed over in his place.

rationale: Both prefer an uncomfortable dwelling to hostile company: 21:19 contrasts desert land with a battling, quick-tempered woman, while 25:24 contrasts a roof corner with an abusive wife.
source_text: Better to dwell in a desert land than with a battling, talkative, and quick-tempered woman.

target_units.text: Better to dwell on a corner of a roof than with an abusive wife in a shared house.

rationale: Treasure resting upon the wise person's mouth corresponds to the righteous tongue pictured as fire-tested silver in 10:20. Both give speech a precious-material image.
source_text: Desirable treasure will rest upon a wise person’s mouth, but foolish men will swallow it down.

target_units.text: The tongue of the righteous is fire-tested silver, but the heart of the impious will fail.

rationale: The way of righteousness and mercy finding life in 21:21 corresponds to the explicit statement in 12:28 that life is in ways of righteousness.
source_text: A way of righteousness and mercy will find life and glory.

target_units.text: In ways of righteousness is life, but the ways of those who remember wrongs lead to death.

rationale: Proverbs describes wisdom overcoming fortified cities; Ecclesiastes describes a wise man delivering a besieged city and judges wisdom better than strength and weapons. The military outcomes differ, but both elevate wisdom over force.
source_text: A wise person mounted fortified cities, and brought down the stronghold in which the impious trusted.

target_units.text: There was a small city with few people in it; a great king might come against it, surround it and build great siegeworks against it,
and he might find in it a poor wise man, who will deliver the city by his wisdom; yet no one remembered that poor man.
I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise, heard quietly, are better than the shouting of rulers in follies.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner will destroy much good.

rationale: Both directly connect guarding one's mouth with keeping one's life; 21:23 adds the tongue and specifies preservation from affliction.
source_text: One who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his life from affliction.

target_units.text: One who guards his own mouth keeps his own life, but one rash with his lips will terrify himself.

rationale: The person who remembers wrongs is called lawless in 21:24; 12:28 assigns the ways of those who remember wrongs to death, against the life of righteousness.
source_text: A rash, self-willed, boastful person is called pestilent, and one who remembers wrongs is lawless.

target_units.text: In ways of righteousness is life, but the ways of those who remember wrongs lead to death.

rationale: The lazy person's killing desires and unwilling hands correspond to 13:4's idle person amid desires, contrasted there with courageous hands engaged in care.
source_text: Desires kill a lazy person, for his hands do not choose to do anything.

target_units.text: Every idle person is amid desires, but the hands of the courageous are engaged in care.

rationale: The righteous person's unsparing mercy and compassion correspond to the righteous showing compassion and mercy in 13:9a, in contrast to deceitful wandering in sin.
source_text: The impious desires evil desires the whole day, but the righteous shows mercy and compassion without sparing.

target_units.text: Deceitful lives wander in sins, but the righteous have compassion and show mercy.

rationale: Both explicitly call the sacrifices of the impious an abomination to the Lord; 21:27 gives their lawless manner of offering as the reason.
source_text: The sacrifices of the impious are an abomination to the Lord, for they offer them lawlessly.

target_units.text: The sacrifices of the impious are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those going straight are acceptable to Him.

rationale: The false witness who perishes in 21:28 corresponds to 19:9's warning that a false witness will not escape punishment and that kindled wickedness consumes its instigator.
source_text: A false witness will perish, but an obedient man will speak with caution.

target_units.text: A false witness will not be unpunished, and whoever kindles wickedness will perish by it.

rationale: The upright person's understanding of his ways in 21:29 corresponds to the resourceful person's wisdom recognizing his ways in 14:8.
source_text: An impious man stands his ground with a shameless face, but the upright himself understands his ways.

target_units.text: The wisdom of resourceful people will recognize their ways, but the senselessness of fools is in wandering.

rationale: The absence of wisdom and counsel with the impious corresponds to seeking wisdom among evil people and not finding it in 14:6.
source_text: There is no wisdom, there is no courage, there is no counsel with the impious.

target_units.text: You will seek wisdom among evil people and not find it, but discernment is readily found among intelligent people.

rationale: The prepared warhorse is distinguished from help that comes from the Lord in Proverbs; the psalm contrasts reliance on horses and chariots with the Lord's name, followed by falling or being raised upright.
source_text: A horse is prepared for a day of war, but help is from the Lord.

target_units.text: These rely on chariots, and those on horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God.
They were fettered and fell, but we rose and were set upright.

rationale: Proverbs prefers a good name to much wealth and favor to precious metals; Ecclesiastes similarly ranks a name above good oil.
source_text: A good name is more desirable than much wealth, and good favor is above silver and gold.

target_units.text: A name is better than good oil, and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.

rationale: The proverb says God made both rich and poor; Job appeals to shared formation in the womb when considering his servants' legal case. Both set differences of status beside common human origin.
source_text: Rich and poor met one another, and the Lord made both.

target_units.text: If I also despised the case of my manservant or maidservant when they were in judgment against me,
what will I do if the Lord makes an examination of me? If He also makes an inspection, what answer will I make?
Were they not also formed in the womb just as I was? We were formed in the same belly.

rationale: The resourceful observer instructed by an evil person's punishment corresponds to the fool made more resourceful by watching a pestilent person whipped in 19:25.
source_text: A resourceful person, seeing an evil person severely punished, is himself instructed, but fools passed by and were penalized.

target_units.text: When a pestilent person is whipped, a fool becomes more resourceful; but if you reprove an intelligent man, he will understand discernment.

rationale: Wisdom's offspring include wealth, glory and life in 22:4; 3:16 likewise places length of life, wealth and glory with wisdom.
source_text: The offspring of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and wealth and glory and life.

target_units.text: For length of life and years of living are in her right hand, and wealth and glory in her left.

rationale: Avoiding the thistles and traps of crooked ways preserves life in 22:5; 16:17 similarly connects turning from evil and guarding one's ways with keeping one's life.
source_text: Thistles and traps are in crooked ways, but one who guards his own life will keep away from them.

target_units.text: Paths of life turn aside from evils, and ways of righteousness are length of life. One who receives discipline will be amid good things, and one who keeps rebukes will be made wise. One who guards his own ways keeps his own life, and one who loves his life will spare his mouth.

rationale: Sowing worthless things and reaping evils corresponds to Paul's principle that a person reaps what he sows, illustrated by corruption reaped from sowing to the flesh.
source_text: One who sows worthless things will reap evils, and he will bring the blow of his works to completion.

target_units.text: Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.
For the one who sows into his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but the one who sows into the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

rationale: God's blessing of the cheerful giving man corresponds closely to Paul's description of God loving a cheerful giver, alongside his rejection of sorrowful or compelled giving.
source_text: God blesses a cheerful and giving man, and He will bring the emptiness of his works to an end.

target_units.text: Let each give as he has decided in his heart, not out of sorrow or compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver.

rationale: The person who shared loaves with the poor is promised nourishment in 22:9; 28:27 similarly promises that giving to the poor will not leave the giver in need.
source_text: One who has mercy on the poor will himself be nourished, for he gave of his own loaves to the poor.

target_units.text: One who gives to the poor will not be in need; but one who turns away his eye will be in great difficulty.

rationale: Proverbs 22:9a says the giver takes away the life of those possessing the gifts; 15:27 similarly connects taking bribes with the recipient's destruction, although 22:9a also describes honor for the giver.
source_text: One who has given gifts obtains victory and honor, yet takes away the life of those who possess them.

target_units.text: One who takes bribes destroys himself, but one who hates taking gifts is saved.

rationale: Expelling a pestilent council member sends strife away in 22:10; 26:20 likewise says battle becomes quiet where the double-minded person is absent, using firewood as its analogy.
source_text: Cast a pestilent person out of a council, and strife will go out with him; for whenever he sits in a council, he dishonors everyone.

target_units.text: With much wood a fire flourishes, but where there is no double-minded person, battle is quiet.

rationale: The Lord's love of devout hearts and acceptance of the blameless correspond to 11:20's acceptance before Him of those blameless in their ways.
source_text: The Lord loves devout hearts, and all the blameless are acceptable to Him; a king shepherds with his lips.

target_units.text: Perverted ways are an abomination to the Lord, but all who are blameless in their ways are acceptable to Him.

rationale: Both put the excuse of a lion in the roads in the lazy person's mouth; 22:13 adds murderers in the squares.
source_text: The lazy person makes an excuse and says, “A lion is in the roads, and murderers in the squares!”

target_units.text: A lazy person sent on a journey says, “A lion is in the roads!”

rationale: The lawless person's mouth is a deep pit into which someone falls in 22:14; 11:9 similarly places a trap for citizens in the impious person's mouth.
source_text: The mouth of a lawless person is a deep pit, and one hated by the Lord will fall into it.

target_units.text: In the mouth of the impious is a trap for citizens, but the discernment of the righteous has a good course.

rationale: The command to turn from a crooked and evil way in 22:14a corresponds to 4:27's instruction to turn one's foot away from an evil way.
source_text: There are evil ways before a man, and he does not love turning from them; but one must turn from a crooked and evil way.

target_units.text: Do not turn to the right or the left; turn your foot away from an evil way.

rationale: Proverbs 22:15 puts a young person's attached senselessness beside the distance of rod and discipline; 29:15 conversely assigns wisdom to blows and reproofs and describes the shame of a wandering child.
source_text: Senselessness is fastened to a young person’s heart, but rod and discipline are far from him.

target_units.text: Blows and reproofs give wisdom, but a wandering child shames his parents.

rationale: Both describe extortion from the poor: 22:16 describes the extorter's increased goods and losses in giving to the rich, while 28:3 identifies extortion as the practice of an impious man.
source_text: One who extorts from the needy makes his own things many, but gives to the rich at a loss.

target_units.text: A man vigorous in impieties extorts the poor. Just like a violent and useless rain,

rationale: Both direct the learner to apply the ear to the teacher's words and connect this hearing with the heart: understanding their goodness in 22:17 and retaining them in 4:21.
source_text: Bring your ear beside words of the wise and hear my word, and direct your heart so that you may know that they are good;

target_units.text: Son, attend to my utterance; apply your ear to my words,
so that your springs do not fail you; keep them in your heart,

rationale: Putting the wise words into the heart in 22:18 corresponds to writing commands on the breadth of the heart in 7:3; 22:18 adds their glad expression upon the lips.
source_text: and if you put them into your heart, they will gladden you together upon your lips,

target_units.text: Put them around your fingers; inscribe them on the broad surface of your heart.

rationale: Hope in the Lord corresponds to 3:5's command to trust God with one's whole heart and not exalt oneself in one's own wisdom.
source_text: so that your hope may be in the Lord, and He may make His way known to you.

target_units.text: Trust God with your whole heart; do not exalt yourself in your own wisdom.

rationale: The direction to copy the teachings threefold for counsel and knowledge upon the heart corresponds to 7:3's instruction to write the commands on the breadth of one's heart.
source_text: And you, copy them for yourself threefold, for counsel and knowledge upon the breadth of your heart.

target_units.text: Put them around your fingers; inscribe them on the broad surface of your heart.

rationale: The teacher supplies true words and knowledge so the learner can answer questioners truthfully; Colossians similarly connects cultivated gracious speech with knowing how to answer each person.
source_text: Therefore I teach you to heed a true word and good knowledge, so as to answer words of truth to those who put questions to you.

target_units.text: Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

relationship: protection of the poor in judgment
rationale: The prohibition on using force against the needy and dishonoring the weak at the gates corresponds to Exodus's prohibition on perverting a poor person's judgment in his case.
source_text: Do not use force against the needy, for he is poor, and do not dishonor the weak at the gates;

target_units.text: You shall not pervert the judgment of a poor man in his cause.

rationale: The Lord judging the poor person's case corresponds to the mighty Lord who redeems the orphans and judges their case in 23:11.
source_text: for the Lord will judge his case, and you will preserve your own life unplundered.

target_units.text: for the Lord who redeems them is mighty, and He will judge their case with you.

rationale: The warning against lodging with an angry friend can be read with 15:18's explanation that a quick-tempered man prepares battles, unlike the patient person who calms them.
source_text: Do not be a companion to a quick-tempered man, and do not lodge with an angry friend,

target_units.text: A quick-tempered man prepares battles, but a patient person calms even a battle about to begin.

rationale: The danger of learning an angry companion's ways corresponds to Sirach's warning that one who associates with a proud person becomes like him, illustrated by touching staining pitch.
source_text: lest you learn his ways and take nooses for your own life.

target_units.text: The one who touches pitch will be stained, and the one who associates with a proud person will become like him.

rationale: The warning against giving oneself as a pledge corresponds to the son's guarantee in 6:1-3, giving his hand over to an enemy, entrapment by his own lips and the command to seek release.
source_text: Do not give yourself as a pledge out of deference to a face.

target_units.text: Son, if you act as guarantor for your friend, you will give your hand over to an enemy.
For a man’s own lips are a strong trap, and he is caught by the lips of his own mouth.
Son, do what I command you and save yourself—for through your friend you have come into evil men’s hands. Go without growing slack, and press the friend for whom you acted as guarantor.

rationale: Proverbs warns that inability to pay can cost the debtor his bedding; Exodus requires a pledged garment to be returned before sunset because it is the person's only covering for sleep.
source_text: For if you have no means from which to pay, they will take the bedding from beneath your sides.

target_units.text: And if you take your neighbour’s garment in pledge, you shall restore it to him before the setting of the sun;
for this is his covering, his only garment for his nakedness; What shall he sleep in? If therefore he cries to Me, I will listen to him; for I am merciful.

rationale: Both forbid moving the boundaries set by one's fathers; Deuteronomy places this protection in the context of the allotted inheritance in the land.
source_text: Do not move everlasting boundaries that your fathers set.

target_units.text: You shall not remove your neighbour’s boundaries, which your fathers set in your inheritance, which was allotted unto you in the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession.

rationale: The perceptive worker standing beside kings corresponds to the intelligent attendant acceptable to a king and removing dishonor by skill in 14:35.
source_text: A perceptive man, keen in his works, must stand beside kings and not stand beside sluggish men.

target_units.text: An intelligent attendant is acceptable to a king, and by his own skill he removes dishonor.

rationale: Thoughtfully considering the food at rulers' tables corresponds to Sirach's instruction to consider matters at a great table and eat what is set before one without greedy grasping.
source_text: If you sit to dine at the table of rulers, thoughtfully consider what is set before you,

target_units.text: Have you sat at a great table? Do not open your throat over it or say, “How much there is upon it!”
Remember that an evil eye is bad. What has been created worse than an eye? Therefore it weeps for every reason.
Do not stretch your hand toward whatever it looks at, and do not crowd together with it in the dish.
Understand your neighbor’s concerns from yourself, and consider every matter.
Eat what is set before you like a human being, and do not chew greedily, lest you be hated.

rationale: The warning not to desire a ruler's food out of insatiability corresponds to Sirach's instruction not to chew greedily and to stop for discipline rather than become insatiable.
source_text: but if you are more insatiable, do not desire his foods, for these belong to a false life.

target_units.text: Eat what is set before you like a human being, and do not chew greedily, lest you be hated.
Be the first to stop for the sake of good discipline; do not be insatiable, lest you stumble.

rationale: Proverbs tells the poor person not to stretch himself to match the rich; Sirach similarly warns against a burden beyond oneself and association with someone stronger and richer, using unequal pots as an image.
source_text: Do not stretch yourself, being poor, to match a rich man, but hold back in your own reflection;

target_units.text: Do not lift a burden beyond you, and do not associate with someone stronger and richer than you. What fellowship can an earthen pot have with a cauldron? One will strike, and the other will be shattered.

rationale: Avoiding the begrudging host's desirable food corresponds to the preference in 15:17 for vegetables with friendship over calves with enmity.
source_text: Do not dine with a begrudging man, and do not desire his foods,

target_units.text: Better hospitality of vegetables with friendship and favor than a serving of calves with enmity.

rationale: The fool's sneering at intelligent words corresponds to the uneducated person's refusal to love a reprover or associate with the wise in 15:12.
source_text: Say nothing into a fool’s ears, lest he sneer at your intelligent words.

target_units.text: An uneducated person will not love those who reprove him, and he will not associate with the wise.

rationale: The prohibition on moving everlasting boundaries corresponds to Deuteronomy's prohibition on removing ancestral boundaries of the allotted inheritance; Proverbs also specifically protects orphans' property.
source_text: Do not move everlasting boundaries, and do not enter orphans’ property,

target_units.text: You shall not remove your neighbour’s boundaries, which your fathers set in your inheritance, which was allotted unto you in the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession.

rationale: The mighty Lord who redeems orphans and judges their case corresponds to the Lord judging the poor person's case in 22:23.
source_text: for the Lord who redeems them is mighty, and He will judge their case with you.

target_units.text: for the Lord will judge his case, and you will preserve your own life unplundered.

relationship: heart and ear applied to wisdom
rationale: Both combine giving the heart to instruction or understanding with preparing or applying the ear to wisdom and discernment.
source_text: Give your heart to discipline, and prepare your ears for words of discernment.

target_units.text: your ear will obey wisdom, and you will apply your heart to understanding; you will also apply it to admonishing your son.

rationale: The instruction not to refrain from disciplining a child with a rod corresponds to 13:24's contrast between sparing the staff and the careful discipline associated with parental love.
source_text: Do not refrain from disciplining a little child, for if you strike him with a rod, he will certainly not die;

target_units.text: One who spares the staff hates his son, but one who loves him disciplines carefully.

rationale: The rod is presented as rescuing the child's life in 23:14; 13:24 likewise presents careful discipline with the staff as an expression of love for one's son.
source_text: for you will strike him with a rod, but rescue his life from death.

target_units.text: One who spares the staff hates his son, but one who loves him disciplines carefully.

rationale: The child's wise heart gladdening the speaker's heart corresponds to 27:11's direct appeal that the son become wise so the parent's heart may rejoice.
source_text: Son, if your heart becomes wise, you will gladden my heart too,

target_units.text: Become wise, son, so that my heart may rejoice, and turn reproachful words away from yourself.

rationale: Both directly prohibit envy of evil people or sinners; 23:17 contrasts this with continual fear of the Lord, while 24:1 also rejects desire for their company.
source_text: Do not let your heart envy sinners, but be in the fear of the Lord the whole day;

target_units.text: Son, do not envy evil men, and do not desire to be with them;

rationale: The promise that hope will not depart when the prior instruction is kept corresponds to 24:14's promise that finding wisdom brings a good end and hope that does not abandon the learner.
source_text: for if you keep these things, you will have offspring, and your hope will not depart.

target_units.text: in this way you will perceive wisdom for your own life; for if you find it, your end will be good, and hope will not abandon you.

rationale: Both directly address the son and command listening so that he may become wise; 23:19 also calls for straightened reflections, while 19:20 looks to wisdom in later days.
source_text: Listen, son, and become wise, and straighten the reflections of your heart.

target_units.text: Listen, son, to your father’s discipline, so that you may become wise in your latter days.

rationale: The warning against becoming a wine-drinker can be read with Paul's prohibition on drunkenness with wine because of its reckless excess; the latter specifically contrasts drunkenness with being filled in the Spirit.
source_text: Do not be a wine-drinker, and do not stretch yourself over contributions and purchases of meat;

target_units.text: And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is reckless excess, but be filled in the Spirit,

rationale: The prediction that a frequenter of prostitutes becomes poor corresponds to 29:3's statement that tending prostitutes destroys wealth; 23:21 includes drunkards and sleepy people in its warning as well.
source_text: for every drunkard and frequenter of prostitutes will become poor, and every sleepy person will clothe himself in torn and ragged things.

target_units.text: When a man loves wisdom, his father rejoices; but one who tends prostitutes will destroy wealth.

rationale: The command not to despise a mother because she has grown old corresponds to 30:17's warning against the eye that dishonors a mother's old age and mocks a father.
source_text: Listen, son, to the father who begot you, and do not despise your mother because she has grown old.

target_units.text: An eye mocking a father and dishonoring a mother’s old age—may ravens from the ravines peck it out, and may young eagles devour it.

rationale: The father's rejoicing over a wise son corresponds directly to 10:1's statement that a wise son makes his father glad.
source_text: A righteous father brings up well, and his life rejoices over a wise son;

target_units.text: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is grief to his mother.

rationale: The call for father and mother to rejoice over the child corresponds to 17:21's contrast between a father's lack of joy over an uneducated son and the intelligent son gladdening his mother.
source_text: let father and mother rejoice over you, and let the one who bore you be glad.

target_units.text: and a fool’s heart is pain to the one who possesses it. A father does not rejoice over an uneducated son, but an intelligent son gladdens his mother.

rationale: Giving the heart and keeping the teacher's ways with one's eyes corresponds to 4:23-26's coordinated commands to guard the heart, direct the eyes toward righteousness and straighten one's tracks.
source_text: Give me your heart, son, and let your eyes keep my ways;

target_units.text: With every guard keep your heart, for from these come life’s outlets.
Remove a crooked mouth from yourself and thrust unjust lips far away from you.
Let your eyes look straight, and let your eyelids incline toward righteous things.
Make straight tracks for your feet and direct your ways rightly.

rationale: Proverbs 23:27 describes another's well as narrow alongside the leaking jar image of another's house; 9:18c likewise warns away from foreign water and drinking from a foreign spring.
source_text: for another’s house is a jar with holes, and another’s well is narrow;

target_units.text: But keep away from foreign water, and do not drink from a foreign spring,

rationale: The uproar, lawsuits and gratuitous bruises of 23:29, attributed to drinkers in its following verse, correspond to Sirach's description of excessive wine bringing conflict, anger and wounds.
source_text: Who has woe? Who has uproar? Who has a lawsuit? Who has unpleasantness and chatter? Who has bruises for nothing? Whose eyes are livid?

target_units.text: Wine drunk in quantity amid provocation and conflict is bitterness of soul.
Drunkenness multiplies a fool’s anger to his stumbling, diminishing strength and adding wounds.

rationale: The people lingering over wine and seeking drinking parties correspond to Isaiah's drinkers who pursue strong drink from morning into evening and neglect the Lord's works.
source_text: Is it not those who linger over wines? Is it not those who track down where drinking parties take place?

target_units.text: Woe to those rising in the morning and pursuing strong drink, lingering into the evening, for wine will burn them up!
For with lyre and harp, drums and flutes they drink wine, but they do not look at the Lord’s works or consider the works of His hands.

rationale: Both explicitly command against becoming drunk with wine; Proverbs then urges company with righteous people, while Ephesians directs being filled in the Spirit.
source_text: Do not become drunk with wine, but associate with righteous people, and converse during walks; for if you give your eyes to bowls and cups, afterward you will walk about barer than a pestle.

target_units.text: And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is reckless excess, but be filled in the Spirit,

rationale: In the continuing portrait of the drinker, Proverbs pictures collapse and spreading poison like a snakebite; Sirach likewise warns that wine destroys many and that drunkenness diminishes strength and adds wounds.
source_text: But at the end he lies stretched out as though struck by a snake, and as though by a horned viper its poison spreads through him.

target_units.text: Do not show your manliness with wine, for wine has destroyed many.
A furnace tests hardened metal in quenching; so wine tests hearts in the quarrel of the proud.
Wine is like life for human beings if you drink it in its measure. What is life for someone lacking wine? It too was created for human gladness.
Wine drunk at the proper time in sufficient measure is rejoicing of heart and gladness of soul.
Wine drunk in quantity amid provocation and conflict is bitterness of soul.
Drunkenness multiplies a fool’s anger to his stumbling, diminishing strength and adding wounds.

rationale: The drinker's eyes on another woman and ensuing crooked words contrast with 4:24-25's commands to remove a crooked mouth and direct the eyes toward righteous things.
source_text: When your eyes see another woman, then your mouth will speak crooked things,

target_units.text: Remove a crooked mouth from yourself and thrust unjust lips far away from you.
Let your eyes look straight, and let your eyelids incline toward righteous things.

rationale: Proverbs compares the drinker's condition to a helmsman in heavy seas; the psalm conversely compares storm-tossed sailors' shaking and loss of wisdom to a drunken man.
source_text: and you will lie down as in the heart of the sea, and like a helmsman in heavy surging;

target_units.text: He spoke, and a storm wind stood, and its waves were raised.
They rise as far as the heavens and descend as far as the deeps; their soul melted in evils.
They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.

rationale: After unperceived blows and mockery, the drinker plans to seek his companions again; 26:11 similarly pictures a fool returning to his wicked sin, compared there to a dog encountering its own vomit.
source_text: and you will say, “They strike me, and I felt no pain; they mocked me, but I did not know. When will dawn come, so that I may go and seek those with whom I will gather?”

target_units.text: Like a dog that comes upon its own vomit and becomes hateful is a fool who has returned in his own wickedness to his own sin.
